A former physics teacher turned politician, this four-term Turkish MP ran as the main opposition's presidential candidate in 2018, finishing second to the incumbent with just over 30% of the vote — who is he?
Muharrem İnce: Turkish politician. Muharrem İnce (Turkish: [inˈdʒe]; born 4 May 1964) is a Turkish physics teacher, school principal, sport executive, and politician.

Serving as Turkey's 23rd prime minister from 1996 to 1997, this Islamist politician was later banned from politics for violating the constitution's secularism clause after founding a movement called Millî Görüş — who is he?
Necmettin Erbakan: Prime Minister of Turkey from 1996 to 1997.
Founded by Nayib Bukele in 2017, this party now holds near-unanimous control of El Salvador's Legislative Assembly — which party?
Nuevas Ideas: Political party in El Salvador. Nuevas Ideas (English: New Ideas; abbreviated N or NI) is the current ruling political party of El Salvador.
Hebrew for 'Jewish Power,' this far-right Israeli political party grew out of the banned Kach movement and was linked in its early years to politician Itamar Ben-Gvir — which party?
Otzma Yehudit: Israeli far-right political party. Otzma ran independently in the 2013 election and as part of a list with ultra-Orthodox party Yachad in 2015.
Based on the doctrine of a 20th-century Argentine leader, this political movement is defined by three 'flags' — social justice, economic independence, and political sovereignty — what is it called?
Peronism: Argentine political movement. Peronism, also known as justicialism, is an Argentine ideology and political movement, based on the ideas, doctrine, and legacy of Juan Perón (1895–1974).

The first person from West Bengal to become President of India, this longtime Congress leader had been Finance Minister just before his 2012 election and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2019. Who is he?
Pranab Mukherjee: President of India from 2012 to 2017. Prior to his election as President, Mukherjee was Finance Minister from 2009 to 2012 also in 1982 to 1984.
This Indian politician became Minister of Defence in 2019 and was the first person born after independence to serve as Union Minister of Home Affairs — who is he?
Rajnath Singh: Defense Minister of India since 2019.
Going by his initials 'rms,' this programmer launched the GNU Project, founded the Free Software Foundation, and wrote every version of the GNU General Public License — who is he?
Richard Stallman: American activist and programmer (born 1953)
Orphaned of his murdered father at age two, this Shia cleric grew up to lead a revolution that toppled the Shah and made him his country's first supreme leader — who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini: Supreme Leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989.
This French economist and Green party lawmaker, representing a Paris constituency since 2022, became a leading voice of France's version of the Me Too movement — who is she?
Sandrine Rousseau: French economist and politician. Rousseau previously served as a vice-president of the University of Lille.
At 35, he became Russia's youngest-ever prime minister in 1998 and later ran the Rosatom nuclear agency for over a decade — who is this Kremlin technocrat?
Sergey Kiriyenko: Prime Minister of Russia In 1998.
A Jagiellonian king of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506, he earned his "the Old" nickname only later, to tell him apart from the son who succeeded him. Who was this monarch?
Sigismund I the Old: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506 to 1548. Sigismund was born in the town of Kozienice in 1467 as the fifth son of Casimir IV and Elizabeth of Austria.
The only prime minister to date from the modern Conservative Party of Canada, this Calgary economist co-founded the party and led the country from 2006 to 2015 — who is he?
Stephen Harper: Prime Minister of Canada from 2006 to 2015. Stephen Joseph Harper (born April 30, 1959) is a Canadian politician who served as the 22nd prime minister of Canada from 2006 to 2015.
Its Sanskrit name evokes weaving or a loom, and this occult Hindu tradition views the body as divine, seeking the union of the god Shiva and his consort — what is it called?
Tantra: Esoteric traditions of Hinduism and Buddhism.
Around the year 1010, this Icelandic explorer followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland with his wife Gudrid in a short-lived bid to found a permanent settlement — who was he?
Serving as ealdorman of Northumbria from 1006 until his assassination in 1016, this ruler's death sparked a blood feud with Thurbrand the Hold — who was he?
This Hungarian lawyer-politician has led the Fidesz party and served as prime minister twice, taking the country into NATO during his first stint. Who is he?
Viktor Orbán: Prime Minister of Hungary (1998–2002, 2010–2026)
This early American writer gave us 'Rip Van Winkle' and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,' and later served as the U.S. ambassador to Spain — who was he?
Washington Irving: American writer, historian and diplomat (1783–1859)
The only Democrat elected president during the Republican-dominated Progressive Era, he steered the U.S. through World War I and championed the League of Nations — which 28th president was he?
Woodrow Wilson: President of the United States from 1913 to 1921.
A close associate of Gandhi and a founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, this Berlin-educated educationist rose to become president of India, dying in office in 1969 — who was he?
Zakir Husain: President of India from 1967 to 1969.
Which of these people was born first?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Saint Valentine (born 175) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Bash (Unix shell) (founded 1989) is the earliest of the four.
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Stephen Gray (scientist) is an astronomer. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen is a mathematician. Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (born Nicolae Georgescu, 4 February 1906 – 30 October 1994) was a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist.
What is the atomic number of Dubnium?
Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
What is the atomic number of Iridium?
Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
In what year was B. R. Ambedkar born?
B. R. Ambedkar: Ambedkar served as Law and Justice minister in the first cabinet of Jawaharlal Nehru.
In what year was Hedy Lamarr born?
Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler; November 9, 1914 – January 19, 2000) was an Austrian and American actress and inventor.
In what year was Erwin Schrödinger born?
Erwin Schrödinger: Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac "for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory".
In what year did William Howard Taft die?
William Howard Taft: Taft attended Yale and joined Skull and Bones, of which his father was a founding member.
In what year did Karl Marx die?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year was Fluorine discovered?
Fluorine is a chemical element; it has symbol F and atomic number 9.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.
Which country is Panavia Tornado from?
Panavia Tornado: Italy. It first flew on 14 August 1974 and was introduced into service in 1979–1980.
Who is credited with discovering Phoenix?
Phoenix (constellation): Petrus Plancius. Named after the mythical phoenix, it was first depicted on a celestial atlas by Johann Bayer in his 1603 Uranometria.
Who is credited with discovering Glycerol?
Glycerol: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Glycerol is a sugar alcohol with chemical formula C3H5(OH)3.
Who is credited with discovering Theory of relativity?
Theory of relativity: Albert Einstein. Special relativity applies to all physical phenomena in the absence of gravity.
Who is credited with discovering Sombrero Galaxy?
Sombrero Galaxy: Pierre Méchain. It is a member of the Virgo II Groups, a series of galaxies and galaxy clusters strung out from the southern edge of the Virgo Supercluster.
In chemistry, this class is defined by an −OH group that lends water-loving properties to otherwise water-shy hydrocarbons, spanning everything from ethanol to sugar versions — what is it?
Alcohol (chemistry) (from Arabic al-kul 'the kohl') is a type of organic compound that carries at least one hydroxyl (OH) functional group bound to a saturated carbon atom.
A balloon-like bulge at a weakened patch of vessel wall, it can turn lethal in the brain's circle of Willis or the aorta if it bursts — what is this?
Aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.
This deciduous shrub genus in the rose family comes in black, red, and hybrid purple berry varieties, all bitter enough to usually be processed rather than eaten fresh — which genus?
Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
This large bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists mostly — 70 to 90 percent — of bone. What bird is it?
Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.
Dermatologists call the small version of this fluid-filled skin pocket a vesicle and the larger version a bulla; its English name traces back to an Old French word for a leprous nodule. What is it?

Blister is a small pocket of body fluid (lymph, serum, plasma, blood, or pus) within the upper layers of the skin, usually caused by forceful rubbing (friction), burning, freezing, chemical exposure or infection.

More muscular and aggressive than the females of the species, this uncastrated adult male of Bos taurus has long symbolized power in religious sacrifice and features prominently in ranching and blood sports — which term describes him?
Bull is an intact (i.e., not castrated) adult male of the species Bos taurus (cattle).

Born in London and raised in Milan, this Italian Catholic teenager taught himself computer programming and web design to promote devotion to the Eucharist online before his death in 2006 at age 15 — who was he?
Carlo Acutis (3 May 1991 - 12 October 2006) was an English-born Italian Catholic teenager known for his devotion to the Eucharist and his use of digital media to promote Catholic devotion.
This plant-cell organelle uses chlorophyll pigments to capture sunlight and convert it into chemical energy, ultimately producing sugar via the Calvin cycle — what is it?
Chloroplast (-plahst) is a type of organelle known as a plastid that conducts photosynthesis mostly in plant and algal cells.
A true thrush of Europe, western Asia and North Africa, the male of its nominate subspecies is entirely black — and depending on latitude it may stay put or migrate. What bird is it?
Common blackbird (Turdus merula) is a species of true thrush.
A creeping vine of the gourd family that originated across Asia from India to Yunnan, this annual comes in slicing, pickling, and seedless types — what is it?
Cucumber (Cucumis sativus) is a widely-cultivated creeping vine plant in the family Cucurbitaceae that bears cylindrical to spherical fruits, used as culinary vegetables.

Lean, fast, and wedge-skulled, this medium-sized Australian canine comes in ginger, black-and-tan, or creamy white, and scientists still argue whether it's a dog, a wolf subspecies, or its own species — what is it?
Dingo is a lineage of dog found in Australia.

This scientific and engineering discipline uses transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits to control and amplify the flow of electric current, converting between forms like AC to DC. What is the field called?

Electronics is a scientific and engineering discipline that studies and applies the principles of physics to design, create, and operate devices that manipulate electrons and other electrically charged particles.
This U.S. Marine turned professor wrote a 1981 memoir of his WWII combat, later adapted into a Ken Burns documentary and an HBO miniseries where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who was he?
Eugene Sledge (November 4, 1923 - March 3, 2001) was a United States Marine, university professor, and author.
Found at the terminal end of the limb in many vertebrates, this weight-bearing anatomical structure enables locomotion and is typically made up of multiple bony segments — what is it?
Foot (pl.: feet) is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. The plural form feet is an instance of i-mutation.
With the symbol Ge and atomic number 32, this lustrous, brittle metalloid was predicted to exist by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, decades before it was actually discovered — name this element?
Germanium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ge and atomic number 32.
This branch of medicine focuses on the female reproductive system, and when combined with the study of pregnancy and childbirth forms the field known as OB-GYN — name the specialty?
Gynaecology (or gynecology in American English) is the area of medicine concerned with conditions affecting the female reproductive system.

First described by an English physician in 1832, this cancer of the lymphocytes is identified by giant multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes, and about half its cases trace back to the Epstein-Barr virus. What is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a cancer where multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells) are present in the lymph nodes.
First used ritually by forager tribes in Central Africa and later adopted by Gabon's Bwiti tradition, this psychoactive plant alkaloid interacts with both opioid and serotonin receptors — what is it?
Ibogaine is a psychoactive indole alkaloid derived from plants such as Tabernanthe iboga, characterized by hallucinogenic and oneirogenic effects.

This American economist gave his name to a model for censored dependent variables — the 'tobit' — and advised the Council of Economic Advisers while championing government action to head off recessions. Who was he?

James Tobin (March 5, 1918 - March 11, 2002) was an American economist who served on the Council of Economic Advisers and consulted with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and taught at Yale University.
This Soviet-designed naval helicopter has spawned variants for assault transport, export, and civilian use, and still flies today from Russia to India -- which aircraft?

Kamov Ka-27 (NATO reporting name 'Helix') is a military helicopter developed for the Soviet Navy, and as of 2024 is in service in various countries including Russia, Ukraine, Vietnam, China, South Korea, and India.
Caused by a specific type of waterborne bacteria, this form of atypical pneumonia brings cough, fever, muscle pain, and headache within days of exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.

Fatigue, memory problems, breathlessness, and sleep trouble that the WHO marks as setting in three months after infection — symptoms that vanish and reappear for weeks or years. What condition is this?
Long COVID is a group of health problems persisting or developing after an initial period of COVID19 from 2 infection.
An autosomal dominant flaw in the fibrillin-making FBN1 gene gives this disorder its tell-tale look — tall, long-limbed, double-jointed — while quietly threatening the aorta — what is it?
Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a multi-systemic genetic disorder that affects the connective tissue.
This medication treats nausea, vomiting, and acid reflux by blocking dopamine receptors, but is rarely recommended for more than twelve weeks due to a risk of movement disorders — what drug is it?
Metoclopramide is a medication used to treat nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease.
A demyelinating disease whose relapsing-remitting form shows up in about 85% of patients, it can cause double vision, muscle weakness, and loss of coordination — what is it?
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin, the insulating cover of nerve cells in the human body, causing damage to one's own central nervous system.
Element 113, a synthetic and ferociously radioactive member of the periodic table, was confirmed by a team at Riken in Japan — what's its name?
Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
This specialized subunit within a biological cell performs a specific function, and may be enclosed in its own membrane or exist without one. What is it?
Organelle is a specialized subunit, within a biological cell, that has a specific function.
First domesticated in Neolithic China and rarely living past twenty years, this deciduous fruit tree also produces a smooth-skinned variety commercially sold as a different fruit — which tree?
Peach (Prunus persica) is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics.

This class of lipid molecules has a water-loving 'head' built around a phosphate group and two water-fearing fatty-acid 'tails' — and forms an essential building block of neuronal membranes in the brain. Name the class of molecule?

Phospholipid are a class of lipids whose molecule has a hydrophilic "head" containing a phosphate group and two hydrophobic "tails" derived from fatty acids, joined by an alcohol residue (usually a glycerol molecule).
Though it looks like a small dolphin, this cetacean is actually more closely related to narwhals and belugas, and can be told apart by its flattened, spade-shaped teeth — what animal is it?
Porpoise are small dolphin-like cetaceans classified under the family Phocoenidae.
This yellow-white fluid forms at sites of infection and inflammation — when trapped in tissue it's called an abscess, and near the skin's surface a pimple — name the substance?
Pus is an exudate, typically white-yellow, yellow, or yellow-brown, formed at the site of inflammation during infections, regardless of cause.
Home to about 200 species — among them the plants we call currants and gooseberries — this genus is the sole member of its own plant family — which genus?
Ribes is a genus of approximately 200 known species of flowering plants, predominantly native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
The FAO/WHO Codex standard recognizes 21 species under this common name for small silvery forage fish, distinguished from their larger 'pilchard' cousins mainly by size — what fish is it?
Sardine are common names for various species of small, oily forage fish in the herring suborder Clupeoidei.

Defined by the American Thoracic Society as a subjective, uncomfortable experience of breathing discomfort that can include chest tightness or a sense of effort to breathe — what is this sensation called?
Shortness of breath (SOB), known as dyspnea (in AmE) or dyspnoea (in BrE), is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough.
First described in 1780, this slender, long-legged antelope of southern Africa wears a white face crossed by a dark stripe from eye to mouth — and both sexes sport backward-curving horns. What is it?
Springbok (Antidorcas marsupialis) is an antelope found mainly in south and southwest Africa.

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The signs and symptoms depend on the stage it presents: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary.

Beloved by biologists for its wild morphological variation and elaborate nest-building, this northern fish tolerates big swings in salinity, living in the sea but breeding in fresh water — what is it?
Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of 30N.
An important food fish found in marine and brackish waters from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this flatfish's Black Sea relatives are now classified as a separate species — which fish?
Turbot is a relatively large species of flatfish in the family Scophthalmidae.
Leading organic chemistry at DuPont's Experimental Station, this troubled chemist not only invented nylon but also helped lay the groundwork for neoprene. Who was he?
Wallace Carothers (April 27, 1896 - April 29, 1937) was an American chemist, inventor, and the leader of organic chemistry at DuPont, who was credited with the invention of nylon.

Nicknamed the 'Sleeping Dragon' during his years in seclusion, this Chinese strategist was sought out three times by a warlord before becoming chancellor of the Shu Han state and, later, regent to its young second emperor — who is he?

Zhuge Liang (181 AD - September or October 234 AD), courtesy name Kongming, was a Chinese statesman and strategist who lived through the collapse of the Eastern Han dynasty and became the principal architect of the Shu Han state.
This nucleoside, a building block of RNA, gives rise to the energy carriers ATP and ADP and is used as an intravenous drug for certain irregular heartbeats — what is it?
Working at a Soviet computing centre in 1985, this engineer designed one of history's most famous puzzle games — yet saw no royalties from it until founding a company around it in 1996. Who is he?
Caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica, this intestinal infection can spread to the liver and trigger abscesses there even without any prior diarrhea — what condition is it?
Amoebiasis: Human disease caused by amoeba protists.
Central to the 18th-century chemical revolution, this French nobleman named oxygen in 1778 and overturned the phlogiston theory of combustion — who is he?
Antoine Lavoisier: French nobleman and chemist (1743–1794)

A physician who began writing stories while studying medicine in Edinburgh, he was knighted in 1902 and created both a famous consulting detective and the dinosaur-filled adventure The Lost World. Who was he?
Arthur Conan Doyle: British writer and physician (1859–1930)
Nicknamed the hay bacterium for its soil habitat, this rod-shaped, spore-forming microbe is the best-studied Gram-positive species and a top industrial source of secreted enzymes — what is it?
Bacillus subtilis: Catalase-positive bacterium. It forms biofilms through the formation of extracellular polymeric matrix containing sugars and proteins.

With his former teacher Alfred North Whitehead, this English philosopher co-wrote Principia Mathematica and, alongside G. E. Moore, led the British 'revolt against idealism.' Who was this founder of analytic philosophy?
Bertrand Russell: English mathematician and philosopher (1872–1970)
Conceived for Pan Am as a jet two-and-a-half times the size of the 707, this wide-body, led by designer Joe Sutter, rolled out of the world's largest building in 1968 — which airliner is it?
Boeing 747: American wide-body four-engined jet long-range aircraft.
Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways typically causes a cough lasting around three weeks and is usually caused by a virus?
Bronchitis: Inflammation of the large airways in the lungs.
Originally defined as the heat needed to raise one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius, this unit of energy in nutrition actually refers to a kilocalorie — what is it?

Calorie: Unit of energy used in nutrition. The small calorie or gram calorie is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius (or one kelvin).
Blending science, aesthetics, and technique, this discipline wrestles with projecting a round world onto flat media while deciding what details to keep or cut — what is it called?
Cartography: Study and practice of making maps.
Beyond the resistance-measuring "bridge" that carries his name, this English inventor also gave us the stereoscope, the English concertina, and the Playfair cipher — who was he?
Charles Wheatstone: English physicist and inventor (1802–1875)

Unlike oysters and mussels, which attach to a surface, or scallops, which live near the bottom, this bivalve mollusk instead burrows into sand or mud on the sea floor — what is it, the namesake of a popular chowder?
Clam: Common name for several kinds of bivalve mollusc.

This medium-sized bird of prey ranges across Europe into northwestern China, hunting rodents like voles from a perch, with northern populations migrating as far as South Africa for winter — what bird is this?
Common buzzard: Species of bird of prey. It is a member of the genus Buteo in the family Accipitridae.
Domesticated in Africa and thriving in sandy, low-rainfall soil, this ancient legume is now grown mostly in Nigeria and Niger, which together supply two-thirds of the world's crop — which plant?
Cowpea: Species of plant. The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
Nicknamed 'dumb cane' because its poisonous sap can temporarily rob you of speech, this shade-tolerant tropical houseplant is native to the New World — which genus?
Dieffenbachia: Genus of plants. Dieffenbachia, commonly known as dumb cane or leopard lily, is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This plant genus in the mallow family produces the world's most famously pungent fruit, alongside eight other edible-fruit-bearing species — which genus?
Durio: Genus of plants. Several species produce an edible fruit known as durian, the most common species being Durio zibethinus, with eight others producing edible fruit.

The heaviest aircraft ever built by its Brazilian manufacturer, this twin-engine jet transport was developed as a derivative of a regional jetliner, similar in role to the C-130 Hercules. Which aircraft?
Embraer C-390 Millennium: Brazilian military transport aircraft/tanker.
The simplest alkene and the most-produced organic compound on Earth, this colorless gas is also a natural plant hormone used to ripen fruit — what is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Fluconazole: Antifungal medication. Fluconazole, sold under the brand name Diflucan among others, is an antifungal medication used for a number of fungal infections.
Named in 1753 from Greek words for 'milk' and 'flower,' this genus of about 20 bulbous perennial species is better known by its common name, snowdrop — what is its scientific genus?
Galanthus: Genus of flowering plants in the family Amaryllidacee.
Found in the Eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, this prized food fish from the porgy family is a cornerstone of European aquaculture — which fish?
Gilt-head bream: Mediterranean fish. It is a highly esteemed food fish and an important species in aquaculture.
Standing up to a meter tall with a white head marked by a black stripe to its crest, this wading bird of Europe, Asia, and Africa hunts motionless beside water — what is it?
Grey heron: Long-legged predatory wading bird.
Powered by a Rolls-Royce Avon turbojet and featuring swept wings, this 1950s RAF fighter set a world air speed record of over 727 mph in September 1953 — which aircraft?
Hawker Hunter: 1950s family of British fighter aircraft.
Overharvested in the 19th century for old-fashioned bloodletting, this European leech remains endangered in many countries today — which species?
Hirudo medicinalis: Species of annelid worm.
Marketed as Buscopan, this anticholinergic medication treats abdominal cramps, bladder and biliary spasms, and can ease respiratory secretions near the end of life — what drug is it?
Hyoscine butylbromide: Anticholinergic medication. It is also used to improve excessive respiratory secretions at the end of life.
An application of computer science, this field covers not just computers and networks but also distribution technologies like television and telephones — what is it?
Information technology: Computer-based technologies. Whisler commented that "the new technology does not yet have a single established name.

While working as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, this Scottish engineer's separate-condenser design transformed Newcomen's steam engine into the machine that powered the Industrial Revolution — who was he?
James Watt: Scottish inventor, engineer and chemist (1736–1819)

A Columbia economist and former World Bank chief economist who won the 2001 Nobel, he champions Georgism and skewers the "free-market fundamentalists" he blames for mismanaging globalization — who is he?
Joseph Stiglitz: American economist and Nobel Laureate (born 1943)
Also called German turnip despite not being related to true turnips, this stout cabbage cultivar can be eaten raw or cooked, stem and leaves alike — what vegetable?
Kohlrabi: Biennial cultivar of wild cabbage.

One of the five big cats in the genus Panthera, this slender, muscular predator wears dark spots clustered into rosettes and is split today into eight recognised subspecies across Africa and Asia — what is it?
Leopard: Species of cat native to Africa and Asia.

A four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft, this American plane is a comprehensive update of an older transport design, with over 500 delivered to 26 operators worldwide as of 2022. What aircraft is this?
Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules: Military transport aircraft. The C-130J is a comprehensive update of the Lockheed C-130 Hercules, with new engines, flight deck, and other systems.
This is the common name for the larva of flies like houseflies and blowflies — though, confusingly, not for baby mosquitoes — what is it called?
This biological term covers the pairing of organisms for sexual reproduction, encompassing everything from copulation to external fertilization in fish and amphibians — what is it?
Mating: Process of pairing in biology.
Sold under the brand name Dolophine, this synthetic opioid is used to manage chronic pain and treat opioid use disorder by relieving cravings and withdrawal. What is it?
Methadone: Opioid analgesic and maintenance therapy.
Medically termed a 'spontaneous abortion,' this is the loss of an embryo or fetus before it can survive independently — distinct from a stillbirth, which occurs after 20 weeks. What is it?
Miscarriage: Natural premature termination of pregnancy.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
Practitioners of this field are sometimes mistaken for mere coin collectors, but they study all means of paying debts — even the horses the Kyrgyz once used as currency. What's the field called?
Numismatics: Study of currencies, coins and paper money.
Described as far back as the 300s BC by Hippocrates, this bone infection most often strikes the spine in adults and the long bones in children — which condition?
Osteomyelitis: Infection of the bones. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.

Native to southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina, this vine produces a round berry that turns yellow or dark purple at maturity, prized for its juicy, seed-filled interior — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Passiflora edulis: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
Named from a Tupi-Guarani word for tobacco filtered through French, this South American flowering plant genus is a garden hybrid favorite — which plant?
Petunia: Genus of flowering plants. The popular flower of the same name derived its epithet from the French, which took the word pétun, 'tobacco', from a Tupi–Guarani language.

Often stereotyped as ferocious predators, these South American freshwater fish actually have varied diets that include plant matter, making them more omnivorous than their reputation suggests. What fish are they?
Piranha: Common name for certain fishes of the family Serrasalmidae.
Chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese all fall under this term for birds domesticated for meat, eggs, or feathers — what is it called?
Poultry: Domesticated birds kept by humans for their eggs, meat or feathers.
Forming the front-most part of the hip bone in vertebrates, this structure is made up of a superior ramus, an inferior ramus, and a body — which bone?
